extracted.intended_audience: readers or students of Victorian philosophical prose / general literary readers
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis/extraction of evaluative principles and normative statements embedded in a literary/philosophical prose excerpt (Carlyle's Sartor Resartus). Focuses on the text's criteria for moral conduct, the value of books, and the writerly/psychological virtues it praises or condemns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint of inward fury / consuming one's choler
rubrics_metrics.description: "To consume your own choler, as some chimneys consume their own smoke; ... is a negative yet no slight virtue" (and similarly: "to keep a whole Satanic School spouting, if it must spout, inaudibly").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text valorizes the ability to internalize anger and madness rather than outwardly displaying it. Keeping extreme passions silent or private is presented as a (negative-form) virtue appropriate to the times. Example phrasing: one may have a 'whole Satanic School' within yet keep it 'inaudibly' spouting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action rather than mere thought
rubrics_metrics.description: "The end of Man is an Action, and not a Thought" (quoted as a fundamental maxim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle (via the narrator) treats action as the primary end of human life — thought without corresponding action is insufficient. This operates as a normative standard: value and evaluate persons and their works by their enactments, not by contemplative thinking alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know what thou canst work at; measure by performance
rubrics_metrics.description: "_Know what thou canst work at_" and the contrast: "Between vague wavering Capability and fixed indubitable Performance, what a difference!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical self-knowledge — understanding one's actual productive capacities — is urged as a realistic reformulation of 'Know thyself.' The text proposes evaluating worth by concrete works and achievements (the 'mirror' in which the spirit discerns itself) rather than vague inner capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncompromising commitment to Truth; abhorrence of Falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Truth!' I cried, 'though the Heavens crush me for following her: no Falsehood! though a whole celestial Lubberland were the price of Apostasy.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and intellectual integrity — an absolute fidelity to truth even at great cost — is presented as a paramount value. The passage frames this as a test of character: one should prefer truth over worldly reward or comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: The supreme value of a true Book (books as lasting, formative works)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wondrous indeed is the virtue of a true Book. ... Thou who art able to write a Book ... Thou too art a Conqueror and Victor; but of the true sort, namely over the Devil: thou too hast built what will outlast all marble and metal..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books are ranked above cities and conquests as cultural products because they persist, transmit skill and spirit, and can change minds across ages. The criterion for greatness in cultural work is the ability to produce a book that endures, persuades, and forms tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasive/talismanic power of books
rubrics_metrics.description: "...every one of which is talismanic and thaumaturgic, for it can persuade men."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A qualitative measure of a book's value is its power to persuade and effect change in readers. The text emphasizes the almost magical capacity of books to transmit spirit and influence generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer living texts (transformative reading) over mere antiquarian spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: "Fool! why journeyest thou wearisomely, in thy antiquarian fervor, to gaze on the stone pyramids... but canst thou not open thy Hebrew BIBLE, then, or even Luther's Version thereof?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle criticizes empty sightseeing and recommends engaging with living, formative texts. The implicit evaluative rule: cultural engagement that seeks spiritual/normative nourishment (reading canonical transformative works) is superior to purely antiquarian curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indignation and defiance (the 'Everlasting No') as a criterion of psychological rebirth
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thus had the EVERLASTING NO (_das ewige Nein_) pealed... and then was it that my whole ME stood up... '_I_ am not thine, but Free, and forever hate thee!' ... It is from this hour that I incline to date my Spiritual New-birth..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats an unequivocal act of refusal and self-assertion ('Everlasting No') as the pivot of a spiritual new-birth. Psychological maturity and the transition to selfhood are measured by the capacity for principled defiance and the establishment of an inner 'centre' from which to act.
